shortExplanation: Reverse the order of the finite harmonic sums. Dividing the resulting formula for each inner sum by its denominator makes the final sum another shifted harmonic sum.
detailedSteps: Write $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}1/j$. In $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_k$, the term $1/j$ occurs once for each $k=j,j+1,\ldots,n$, hence $n+1-j$ times. Therefore $$T_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{n+1-j}{j}=(n+1)S_n-n.$$
Apply the same identity to each term of $U_n$: $T_k/(k+1)=S_{k+1}-1$. Consequently $$U_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(S_{k+1}-1)=T_{n+1}-S_1-n=T_{n+1}-n-1.$$

Thus the displayed four integers satisfy both required identities. They are all positive and less than $10^6$, as required. The problem asks for suitable integers; these formulas establish their existence without requiring a separate uniqueness argument.
keyIdeas: Count the multiplicity of a summand before evaluating a double sum.
Shift the harmonic index so that the divided inner sum simplifies.
commonMistakes: Counting $1/j$ only $n-j$ times rather than $n+1-j$ times.
Forgetting to remove $S_1=1$ when replacing $S_2+\cdots+S_{n+1}$ by $T_{n+1}-1$.
alternativeMethods: Induction proves $T_n=(n+1)S_n-n$ directly. Summing $T_k/(k+1)=S_{k+1}-1$ then finishes the calculation.
difficultyNotes: The numbers are large, but no decimal approximation is needed. A finite-sum identity resolves both parts exactly.

finalAnswer: Six scheduled games with twelve distinct players always exist.
shortExplanation: There must be at least six connected components in the schedule graph. Each contains a game, and games chosen from different components cannot share players.
detailedSteps: Represent each club member by a vertex and each scheduled game by an edge joining its two players. If a pair plays more than once, retain parallel edges; the proof does not require all games to involve different pairs.

A connected component containing $v$ vertices needs at least $v-1$ edges: starting from one vertex, each edge used to reach a new vertex adds at most one vertex. Equivalently, every connected component contains a spanning tree.
Let there be $c$ components, with vertex counts $v_1,\ldots,v_c$. Since there are exactly $20$ vertices and $14$ scheduled edges, $$14\ge\sum_{j=1}^{c}(v_j-1)=20-c,$$ so $c\ge6$.
Every member plays at least once, so there are no isolated vertices. Each component therefore contains an actual scheduled edge. Choose one such edge from each of six different components.
Different components have disjoint vertex sets. The six selected edges thus have twelve distinct endpoints, giving precisely the required six games.
keyIdeas: Count components from the lower bound on edges in a connected graph.
Choose objects from disjoint components to obtain disjoint participants.
commonMistakes: Assuming the schedule graph is connected or is a forest.
Choosing arbitrary games without ensuring their endpoints are distinct.
Overlooking that the no-isolated-member condition ensures every component has an edge.
alternativeMethods: Remove edges lying on cycles until a spanning forest remains. A forest on $20$ vertices with $c$ components has $20-c$ edges; removing edges cannot make its edge count exceed the original $14$.
difficultyNotes: The useful graph invariant is the number of components. A maximum-matching theorem is unnecessary.

finalAnswer: There is a zero $a+bi$ of $P$ with $\boxed{(a^2+b^2+1)^2<4b^2+1}$.
shortExplanation: At $i$, real-root factors have modulus at least one. Pair each nonreal root with its conjugate; one pair must have modulus below one, which is exactly the desired inequality.
detailedSteps: Because $P$ is monic, the fundamental theorem of algebra factors it into terms $z-r$ for real roots and quadratic factors $(z-a-bi)(z-a+bi)$ for nonreal conjugate pairs. Roots are counted with multiplicity. Real coefficients ensure that conjugate roots occur together.
At $z=i$, a real root $r$ contributes $|i-r|=\sqrt{1+r^2}\ge1$. A conjugate pair contributes the nonnegative modulus $|(i-a-bi)(i-a+bi)|$.
The square of the latter contribution is $$\begin{aligned}|(i-a-bi)(i-a+bi)|^2&=[a^2+(1-b)^2][a^2+(1+b)^2]\\&=(a^2+b^2+1)^2-4b^2.\end{aligned}$$

The product of all these moduli equals $|P(i)|<1$. If every conjugate-pair contribution were at least one, the product would be at least one, because all real-root contributions already are. Thus a conjugate pair must have contribution strictly less than one.

For that pair, $P(a+bi)=0$ and $(a^2+b^2+1)^2-4b^2<1$, which rearranges to the required inequality. If the pair contribution is zero, the conclusion still holds; repeated roots also cause no exception.
keyIdeas: Use conjugate pairs to preserve the real-coefficient structure.
Turn a product below one into a small factor.
Square a conjugate-pair modulus to obtain a real algebraic inequality.
commonMistakes: Discarding the monic leading coefficient without checking it.
Claiming an arbitrary individual root near one side of the complex plane suffices, without using its conjugate.
Treating the zero-product case as an exception.
alternativeMethods: Writing a pair factor as $(z-a)^2+b^2$ gives, at $i$, the complex number $(a^2+b^2-1)-2ai$. Its squared modulus $(a^2+b^2-1)^2+4a^2$ equals the same expression used above.
difficultyNotes: The key step is structural: real factors and conjugate-pair factors play different roles. The calculation alone does not establish that a suitable pair exists.

finalAnswer: Line $IO$ meets the interiors of both $AB$ and $BC$.
shortExplanation: The incenter weights the vertices by side lengths; the circumcenter adds the cosine of each opposite angle. Their strict cosine order determines which two barycentric coordinates vanish along the line.
detailedSteps: Put $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$, and $p=a+b+c$. The given inequalities say $a>b>c$, so the opposite angles satisfy $A>B>C$. Since the triangle is acute, $$0<\cos A<\cos B<\cos C.$$

Use normalized barycentric coordinates: a point $(\lambda_A,\lambda_B,\lambda_C)$ represents $\lambda_A A+\lambda_B B+\lambda_C C$, with coordinate sum one. Positive coordinates with one coordinate zero describe the interior of the opposite side.

The incenter has equal distances from all three sides, so its three subtriangle areas are proportional to $a,b,c$. Therefore $I=(a,b,c)/p$. The circumcenter lies inside an acute triangle. If the circumradius is $R$, its distance from $BC$ is $\sqrt{R^2-a^2/4}=R\cos A$. The analogous distances give area ratios $a\cos A:b\cos B:c\cos C$. Hence $$O=\frac{(a\cos A,b\cos B,c\cos C)}{D},\qquad D=a\cos A+b\cos B+c\cos C.$$
The number $D/p$ is a positive weighted mean, so $\cos A<D/p<\cos C$. In particular, $D-p\cos A>0$ and $p\cos C-D>0$. The unequal cosine values also imply $O\ne I$.

Parametrize the line by $X(t)=I+t(O-I)$. At $$t_+=\frac{D}{D-p\cos A},$$ its normalized coordinates are $$X(t_+)=\left(0,\frac{b(\cos B-\cos A)}{D-p\cos A},\frac{c(\cos C-\cos A)}{D-p\cos A}\right).$$ Both remaining coordinates are strictly positive and their sum is one. Thus $X(t_+)$ lies inside $BC$.

In the opposite direction, take $$t_-=-\frac{D}{p\cos C-D}.$$ Then $$X(t_-)=\left(\frac{a(\cos C-\cos A)}{p\cos C-D},\frac{b(\cos C-\cos B)}{p\cos C-D},0\right).$$ Again the two displayed coordinates are positive and sum to one, so $X(t_-)$ lies inside $AB$. Both points are on $IO$, proving the required segment intersections.
keyIdeas: Use barycentric area ratios for the two centers.
Track a line through its three affine coordinates.
Strict side inequalities turn coordinate nonnegativity into interior intersections.
commonMistakes: Proving intersection only with the infinite supporting lines, rather than with the requested segments.
Using circumcenter area ratios for an obtuse triangle without signed areas.
Ignoring the possibility of coincident centers before defining the line; the strict cosine order excludes it here.
alternativeMethods: Place one side on a coordinate axis, compute the two centers from perpendicular bisectors and angle-bisector weights, then solve the two line-side intersections. The barycentric proof packages the same affine calculation without long coordinates.
difficultyNotes: The geometry proof requires the positivity of both nonzero side coordinates. That is the step that distinguishes segment intersections from intersections with extensions.

shortExplanation: First prove that every permitted real solution is positive. Then $F(9/10)=9$ places $u$ below $9/10$, where the polynomial defining $v$ is strictly smaller than the polynomial defining $u$.
detailedSteps: Define $F(x)=x+x^2+\cdots+x^8+10x^9$ and $G(x)=x+x^2+\cdots+x^{10}+10x^{11}$. The given equations are $F(u)=G(v)=8$. We must consider all real solutions, including possible negative ones.
For $x=-t$ with $0<t\le1$, each adjacent pair satisfies $(-t)^{2j-1}+(-t)^{2j}=t^{2j-1}(t-1)\le0$. The final odd-power term is strictly negative, so $F(-t)<0$ and $G(-t)<0$.

For $t>1$, each of the four pairs in $F(-t)$ is less than $t^8$, and each of the five pairs in $G(-t)$ is less than $t^{10}$. Therefore $$F(-t)<4t^8-10t^9<0,\qquad G(-t)<5t^{10}-10t^{11}<0.$$ At zero both polynomials vanish. Thus $u,v>0$.

On $[0,\infty)$, each polynomial is continuous and strictly increasing: all its terms are increasing and its first-power term is strictly increasing. Since $F(0)=G(0)=0$ while $F(1)=18$ and $G(1)=20$, each equation has exactly one real solution, in $(0,1)$.
At $q=9/10$, a geometric sum gives $$F(q)=\frac{q(1-q^8)}{1-q}+10q^9=9(1-q^8)+9q^8=9.$$ Consequently $0<u<9/10$.
Now factor the difference: $$G(x)-F(x)=x^9(10x^2+x-9)=x^9(x+1)(10x-9).$$ At $x=u$ this is strictly negative, so $G(u)<F(u)=8=G(v)$. Strict increase of $G$ therefore implies $u<v$.
keyIdeas: Exclude negative roots before using positive-axis monotonicity.
Choose an exact comparison point where a geometric sum cancels.
Compare the defining polynomials at one root instead of solving either equation.
commonMistakes: Assuming the real roots are positive without proving it.
Inferring root order directly from the degrees.
Approximating both roots numerically and treating the approximation as a proof.
alternativeMethods: Once positivity is established, derivatives give $F\prime(x)>0$ and $G\prime(x)>0$ for $x\ge0$. The same exact threshold and factored-difference argument finish the comparison.
difficultyNotes: The root comparison is short after the domain is justified. The negative-axis exclusion is essential because the original variables are real, not explicitly positive.
